newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek government seen weathering strike wave.
newsitem.headline: Greek government seen weathering strike wave.

text.p: Greece's socialist government looked determined on Tuesday to weather a three-week strike wave which has damaged the economy but posed no real threat to Prime Minister Costas Simitis.
While the government repeated its "no compromise" stand, farmers who have blocked Greece's road network for 20 days lifted a key barricade on the north-south highway, further relaxing their grip.

Doctors, civil servants, diplomats and seamen were on strike before the opening of a five-day debate on Tuesday in parliament on the 1997 austerity budget but disruption was minimal, government officials said.

The protests were supposed to peak with a mass rally outside parliament on Tuesday evening but only about 2,000 people showed up, making little impact among thousands of holiday shoppers and a giant Christmas tree overlooking the parliament building.
About a dozen workers' groups, mostly in the public sector, were on strike on Tuesday against Simitis's tax-heavy budget.
A seamens' walkout, in its second day, halted commercial transport and tourist ferries. The strike may go on for another two days.
Farmers pressing for cheaper fuel and equipment and state subsidies on their products showed signs of fatigue on Tuesday with the nearest blockade of tractors to Athens being lifted.

The farmers have vowed to stay put on two other major road blocks outside the central town of Larissa but traffic is diverted through smaller streets and no shortages have been reported to markets in northern Greece.

"As far as the government is concerned our position is very clear. We shall not give in. There is no room for further concessions to farmers," National Economy Minister Yannos Papandoniou told Reuters Television on Tuesday.
The budget has angered workers by clamping down on state hiring, limiting wage rises for another year, levying new taxes and eliminating hundreds of tax breaks.
Simitis, a staunch pro-European pragmatist, has said the budget was essential to meet economic targets so Greece can join a single European currency by the year 2001.
He has refused to meet any demands and boldly told the farmers he would only meet them after they abandon their crippling road blockades.
The farmers will travel by bus to Athens for a rally on Thursday and push for a meeting with Simitis.
"We will come down to Athens for a protest on Thursday. The responsibility lies with the prime minister and his government," farmers' representative Thanassis Nasikas told television.
Papandoniou said the government was deeply concerned about the effect of the barricades on the economy and hoped there would be a turning point on Thursday after the farmers' rally.
"The consequences are quite substantial," he said. "The government is really very, very worried about the situation. Our our patience is wearing thin."

The blockade has also taken its toll on the government's popularity in public opinion polls. A poll published in Athens newspapers on Tuesday showed Simitis's popularity had dropped to 38 percent from 50 percent in December last year.
